title: Promoted from the Washtub
shortDescription: Orphaned at seven, widowed at nineteen, with a washboard and a little girl to keep, Sarah Breedlove built a hair-care company that employed nearly twenty thousand women. She gave other women work, marched against lynching and built Villa Lewaro on the Hudson so her people could see what their background could not stop.
introduction: On a plantation near Delta, Louisiana, in December 1867, a girl was born into a world that had changed two years earlier and had not yet caught up. Slavery was over. Her parents had been enslaved on that place; she was the first of their children born free. She would still carry water to field hands, push cotton seed into furrows and wash white people's clothes with lye soap and a washboard. Her name was Sarah Breedlove. Decades later, at a business convention in Chicago, she would introduce herself with the words she had earned — promoted from the cotton fields to the washtub, then to the cook kitchen, then into business. This is how those promotions came, and what she did with them.

chapters.heading: A dollar a week
paragraphs: The plantation near Delta had been a staging area for the Union Army during the siege of Vicksburg. Southern Claims Commission and Freedmen's Bureau records describe a camp and hospital there. They do not name the child born on 23 December 1867, but the place is their record: Owen and Minerva Anderson Breedlove, formerly enslaved, sharecropping now, and their first child born free. In the one-room cabin, Sarah carried water to the people in the fields and pushed cotton seed into each furrow. At five she took white people's washing — lye soap, a stick, a washboard — and was paid a dollar a week. It was the work she would one day call the washtub.

When Sarah was seven, both parents died. She crossed the Mississippi to Vicksburg with Louvenia, her older sister, into the house of Louvenia's husband, Jesse Powell. A failed cotton crop had helped send them across the river. The brother-in-law abused her, and at fourteen she married Moses McWilliams to get out of that house. On 6 June 1885 her daughter, Lelia, was born. In 1887 Moses died. Sarah was nineteen, widowed, with a two-year-old child and the same washboard waiting.

Years later, in 1912, she stood before the National Negro Business League in Chicago and gave the climb in three steps: 'I am a woman that came from the cotton fields of the South; I was promoted from there to the wash-tub; then I was promoted to the cook kitchen, and from there I promoted myself into the business of manufacturing hair goods and preparations.' She used 'promoted' the way another woman might use a ledger: every step had been work, none of it a gift. The room applauded.

chapters.heading: The question at the tub
paragraphs: In 1889 Sarah took Lelia to St. Louis, where four of her brothers had set up as barbers. Washerwomen were wanted there. For seventeen years she cooked and took in laundry, sometimes for a dollar and a half a day. At St. Paul African Methodist Episcopal Church she met women who ran businesses and read books. She joined them, and she made up her mind that Lelia would go to the city's public schools. On paper the 1900 census called her Sarah Davis, married to John Davis, her daughter entered as Lellia McWilliams. The marriage did not last. The work did.

One morning, with a heavy wash in front of her, she looked at her arms in soapsuds and asked herself what would happen when her back stiffened and Lelia was grown: 'What are you going to do when you grow old and your back gets stiff? Who is going to take care of your little girl?' That question outlived the wash. It was still there when the business had a factory.

Her brothers' barber shop gave her the first look at hair care. In her thirties her own hair began to come out in patches. At a time when many women washed once a month and indoor plumbing was rare, scalp infections were common. She tried the preparations sold to Black women and found nothing that worked. Annie Turnbo Malone's Poro Company, founded in St. Louis in 1902, sold through agents who showed customers what to do. Sarah sold Malone's tins first in St. Louis, then in Denver. She saw another Black woman turn a preparation into a trade.

She kept a line for the women who would work for her: 'I had to make my own living and my own opportunity! But I made it! Don't sit down and wait for the opportunities to come. Get up and make them!' Her motto was shorter — 'Perseverance is my motto!' — and she meant the early-morning kind. These were not words painted on a wall. They were instructions for women about to knock on their first door.

chapters.heading: The name on the tin
paragraphs: In 1905 she went to Denver with a dollar and fifty cents, an attic room and two days a week of laundry work. The rest of the week she cooked for other people or mixed preparations and carried them from door to door. Early formulas went into a washtub — the same tool that had paid her way in St. Louis. Wonderful Hair Grower, Glossine and Vegetable Shampoo went out with names that told a customer exactly what was wanted. Advertisements in Denver's Colorado Statesmen carried her further than her feet could.

In early 1906 she married Charles Joseph Walker, a newspaper advertising salesman who knew mail order. She put the name customers were already calling her on the tins: Madam C. J. Walker. In a city where a Black woman might be called 'Aunt Sarah' by a stranger, 'Madam' was not decoration. It was a boundary. C. J. organised the mail-order side and helped with the advertising. When he thought ten dollars a day was enough, she was not satisfied: 'But I was convinced that my hair preparation would fill a long-felt want,' she said. They divorced in 1912.

By 1908 she and Lelia had settled in Pittsburgh. Lelia College trained women in the Walker System: clean the scalp, treat the hair, give manicures and massages, keep records, run a beauty business in their own homes. The recruits were schoolteachers, cooks, housewives and washerwomen — women who recognised the arithmetic of a dollar and a half a day. One agent later said Walker had 'opened up a trade for hundreds of colored women to make an honest and profitable living'.

The trade was not a jar on a shelf. It was a woman knocking at a door, showing another woman how to care for her hair, and leaving her with a way to earn. That was the part Sarah had been asking about at the tub.

media.alt: An advertisement showing the two-ounce tin of Madam C. J. Walker's Wonderful Hair Grower
media.caption: Wonderful Hair Grower was Walker's best-selling product. The woman pictured on the tin was Walker herself.
media.credit: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division / Wikimedia Commons — public domain

chapters.heading: She took the floor
paragraphs: In February 1910 the business moved to Indianapolis, a city of eight railways, factories and a Black commercial district. Walker put in a factory, a hair and manicure salon and a training school. Five thousand agents worked the territory; receipts reached seven thousand dollars a week. The mail-order orders C. J. had helped arrange now travelled beyond the city. In 1911 the Madam C. J. Walker Manufacturing Company was incorporated. The census had already recorded Sarah and Charles Walker as 'manufacturer' in 'hair goods' — the goods she had once bought by the tin.

In August 1912 the National Negro Business League met in Chicago. Booker T. Washington's programme had no women on it. Walker sat in the audience. On the last day she stood up anyway. 'Surely you are not going to shut the door in my face,' she said. 'I feel that I am in a business that is a credit to the womanhood of our race.' Then she gave the room her numbers: seven years earlier, $1.50; that year, $18,000; in her Indianapolis hair business altogether, $63,049.

The stenographer kept going as she told them where the money came from. 'I am not ashamed of my past; I am not ashamed of my humble beginning. Don't think that because you have to go down in the wash-tub that you are any less a lady!' The room applauded. Washington did not react. In Philadelphia in 1913 she was a scheduled speaker, and she told that audience what the money was for: 'I have made it possible for many colored women to abandon the wash-tub for more pleasant and profitable occupation.'

By then the company had ten products built around 'cleanliness and loveliness'. Conventions gathered agents from city to city; prizes went to the strongest sellers and to the women who gave the most to their communities. The girl paid a dollar a week in a Louisiana cabin was now giving work to thousands.

media.alt: The Madam C. J. Walker Manufacturing Company building in Indianapolis in 1911
media.caption: The Walker Manufacturing Company in Indianapolis, photographed in 1911, a year after the business moved to the city.
media.credit: Unknown photographer / Indiana Historical Society / Wikimedia Commons — public domain

chapters.heading: A dime at the Isis Theater
paragraphs: At Indianapolis's Isis Theater, a dime offered for a ticket came back across the counter. Admission, the seller said, had risen to twenty-five cents 'only for colored persons.' Walker sued. She also began planning a building on Indiana Avenue where Black customers would not have to ask which door was theirs — a headquarters with a theatre, drug store, beauty shop, ballroom and coffee shop. A'Lelia finished the Walker Building in 1927, eight years after her mother died.

In 1913 Sarah Walker applied for a United States passport and signed it in a firm hand. Passports then carried no photographs, only a description: five feet tall. That same year she took the products to Central America and the Caribbean; in 1914 a ship manifest recorded her return from Cuba. At A'Lelia's urging she bought a Harlem house with living quarters, a beauty salon and a training school. By 1916 she had moved to New York for good, where her daughter was becoming a figure of the Harlem Renaissance.

The Walker Building gave the city something the Isis Theater had refused: a door that opened without an explanation. Its theatre, drug store, beauty shop, ballroom and coffee shop were planned as Black-owned places in a district where Black money was welcome but Black dignity was not always. A'Lelia saw the building finished in 1927. The dime had been returned. The answer was a building.

chapters.heading: Noon at the White House
paragraphs: Wealth gave her a platform, and she used it against the racial violence that had shadowed her people all her life. On 28 July 1917 she helped organise the Silent Protest Parade in New York. Ten thousand Black men, women and children marched, eight hundred of them children. They walked in silence, drums muffled, shoes scraping the pavement. The provocations were fresh: the lynching — a killing by a mob — of seventeen-year-old Jesse Washington in Waco, Texas, on 15 May, and the East St. Louis riot of 2 July.

The parade was not a petition folded in an envelope. It was bodies in the street, and the sound of shoes where music should have been. Walker knew what a public refusal looked like; she had watched a dime come back across a ticket counter in Indianapolis. This refusal was larger. The target was federal power — laws that would make lynching a national crime.

Four days later she took a train to Washington with a delegation led by James Weldon Johnson of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People. John Nail, Fred Moore and the Reverend Frederick Cullen went with her. They had been promised a noon meeting with President Woodrow Wilson. Noon came and went; Wilson was occupied. The delegation handed its petition to Joseph Tumulty, the president's secretary, then walked to Capitol Hill. 'We ask,' the petition said, 'that lynching and mob violence be made a national crime punishable by the laws of the United States.'

On 31 August, more than two hundred Walker agents gathered at Union Baptist Church in Philadelphia. Marian Anderson, then a young singer, performed. The agents telegraphed Wilson about a lynching in Memphis and the East St. Louis riot, where at least thirty-nine African Americans had been killed. Walker's letter of 7 October to Emmett J. Scott, the highest-ranking Black official in the Wilson administration, was blunt: 'You are now in position to become the "Moses" of our race, to lead us out of the darkness into the light of true womanhood and manhood and I believe you will do your duty without fear or favor.'

chapters.heading: A house so they could see
paragraphs: In 1916, while the organising continued, she began a house on five acres at Irvington-on-the-Hudson, overlooking the river. Vertner Woodson Tandy, a Black architect, designed it. Completed in 1918, it held thirty-four rooms and twenty thousand square feet, a great hall, a barrel-vaulted dining room and a carriage house. It cost about $250,000. Enrico Caruso, who visited, named it Villa Lewaro from the first syllables of Lelia Walker Robinson's name.

The neighbours included Jay Gould and John D. Rockefeller. Through the great hall came James Weldon Johnson, W. E. B. Du Bois, Langston Hughes and Zora Neale Hurston. Frederick Douglass's grandson played the violin at the opening. When guests asked why she had built it, Walker answered, in the National Register nomination's words, that it was 'not for her, but for her people in order to see what could be accomplished, no matter what their background.' The house was meant to be seen. The former washerwoman from Delta was now hosting them above the Hudson; her people should know it was possible.

In 1917 a reporter asked about the stories calling her a millionaire. 'I am not a millionaire, but I hope to be some day,' she said, 'not because of the money, but because I could do so much to help my race.' She had already given a thousand dollars to the African-American YMCA in Indianapolis, paid tuition for six students at Tuskegee Institute in Alabama and pledged five thousand dollars to the NAACP's anti-lynching fund. 'I am not satisfied in making money for myself,' she told an interviewer. 'I endeavor to provide employment for hundreds of the women of my race.'

media.alt: Villa Lewaro, the large house Madam C. J. Walker built at Irvington-on-the-Hudson
media.caption: Villa Lewaro as recorded by the Historic American Buildings Survey around 1986. Walker commissioned the house in 1916 and moved in after its completion in 1918.
media.credit: Historic American Buildings Survey / Library of Congress / Wikimedia Commons — public domain

chapters.heading: The song in the music room
paragraphs: On Sunday morning, 25 May 1919, kidney failure stopped her at Villa Lewaro. She was fifty-one. The news went to Black churches in New York and, that afternoon, to a Negro League baseball game in Chicago. At the funeral on 30 May her casket lay in the music room while employees and agents filed past. J. Rosamond Johnson sang 'Since You Went Away', the spiritual he had written with his brother James Weldon. On 3 June she was buried at Woodlawn Cemetery in the Bronx. Fred Moore, J. Rosamond Johnson and Vertner Tandy, who had designed her house, were among her pallbearers.

Her personal fortune was estimated at six or seven hundred thousand dollars; the company was worth more. Her will directed two-thirds of future net profits to charity, and nearly $100,000 went to individuals, schools and orphanages. A'Lelia took over. In 1927 she completed the Walker Building on Indiana Avenue. The company was sold by the estate trustees in 1986. Villa Lewaro became a National Historic Landmark in 1976.

W. E. B. Du Bois wrote in The Crisis that 'it is given to few persons to transform a people in a generation. Yet this was done by the late Madam C. J. Walker... [She] made and deserved a fortune and gave much of it away generously.' The words that began her public life were better. 'Promoted from there to the wash-tub,' she had told the Chicago convention. She had asked, at the tub, who would take care of her little girl when her back grew stiff. She answered by building a business that let thousands of women leave the wash-tub, and a house on the Hudson where their children could see what she had done.

media.alt: The grave of Madam C. J. Walker at Woodlawn Cemetery in the Bronx
media.caption: Walker was buried at Woodlawn Cemetery in the Bronx on 3 June 1919, nine days after her death at Villa Lewaro.

sources.title: Madam C. J. Walker's Rags-to-Riches Story Found in the Holdings of the National Archives
sources.publisher: U.S. National Archives, Pieces of History
sources.note: Supports the 1867 birth near Delta, Louisiana, the formerly enslaved parents Owen and Minerva Breedlove, the first child born free, the Burney plantation's Southern Claims Commission and Freedmen's Bureau records, orphaning at seven, the move to Vicksburg, marriage at fourteen, the 1900 census entry as Sarah Davis with daughter Lellia McWilliams, work for Annie Malone, the 1905 Denver name, the 1910 census occupations, the 1913 passport signed Sarah Walker and five-foot description, the 1914 Cuba manifest, the 1917 anti-lynching petition wording, the 7 October 1917 letter to Emmett J. Scott, and the National Register account of Villa Lewaro, its name and the reason she built it.

sources.title: Two American Entrepreneurs: Madam C. J. Walker and J. C. Penney — Teaching with Historic Places
sources.note: Supports the one-room cabin, carrying water and planting cotton seed, laundry for $1 a week, the 1882 marriage, Lelia's 6 June 1885 birth, Moses's 1887 death, the 1889 St. Louis move, the hair-loss episode, the $1.50 Denver arrival, Wonderful Hair Grower, Glossine and Vegetable Shampoo, the Colorado Statesmen advertising, the 1906 marriage to C. J. Walker, the 'Aunt Sarah'/'Madam' distinction, his ten-dollar-a-day objection and her long-felt-want answer, the 1908 Lelia College in Pittsburgh, the February 1910 Indianapolis factory, mail-order growth beyond Indianapolis, five thousand agents and seven thousand dollars in weekly receipts, the Isis Theater dime incident, the Walker Building plan, her motto and agents' quotation, Du Bois's Crisis tribute, and the preserved 1912 and 1913 National Negro Business League convention transcripts.

sources.title: (H)our History Lesson: Madam C. J. Walker, African American Millionaire, Philanthropist, Activist
sources.note: Supports the December 1867 birth in Delta, marriage at fourteen, Lelia's birth at seventeen, Moses's death in 1887 when Sarah was nineteen, seventeen years supporting herself and her daughter as a laundress, the Denver products and door-to-door work, and the 1916 commissioning of Villa Lewaro.

sources.title: How Business Executive Madam C. J. Walker Became a Powerful Influencer of the Early 20th Century
sources.note: Supports eighteen years as a washerwoman at $1.50 a day, the hair-loss context and the formula ingredients, the two-ounce tin bearing her own image, the 1912 confrontation with Booker T. Washington, the $1,000 gift to the African-American YMCA, support for Black schools, work with the NAACP, the 1 August 1917 delegation to Wilson's secretary and then Capitol Hill, ten products, twenty thousand saleswomen, the 'cleanliness and loveliness' philosophy, the 1917 millionaire denial, the $600,000–$700,000 personal fortune and the 1986 company sale.

sources.title: Madam C.J. Walker
sources.note: Supports the exact 23 December 1867 birth, the sharecropping parents, orphaning at seven, the marriage at fourteen to escape an abusive brother-in-law, Moses's 1887 death, the 1889 St. Louis move, her use of Annie Malone's products and agency, the 1905 Denver move, the Indianapolis factory, the Walker System training, anti-lynching work and $5,000 NAACP donation, six Tuskegee students, kidney failure as the cause of death, and the will directing two-thirds of future net profits to charity.

sources.title: Madam C.J. Walker: A Brief Biographical Essay (by A'Lelia Bundles)
sources.publisher: Madam C. J. Walker official site
sources.note: The official biography by Walker's great-great-granddaughter. Supports the 23 December 1867 birth on the Delta plantation, the sharecropper parents, the orphaning at seven and cotton-field survival, the marriage at fourteen to escape Jesse Powell, Lelia's 6 June 1885 birth, the move to St. Louis, $1.50 washday wages, St. Paul AME Church, women in that church who ran businesses and read, saving to educate Lelia in public schools, and the move to Indianapolis.

sources.title: The facts about Madam C. J. Walker and Annie Malone
sources.note: Supports Walker's sales and training relationship with Annie Malone, the Poro agency in St. Louis and Denver, the 1906 rift, the product-name overlap, and the estimates of $600,000–$700,000 personal wealth with greater company value. Records the absence of proof for formula-theft claims.

sources.title: Harlem delegation visits White House to protest lynching, August 1, 1917
sources.note: Supports the 28 July 1917 Silent Protest Parade's ten thousand marchers and eight hundred children, the Waco lynching of Jesse Washington and the East St. Louis riot, the 1 August delegation led by James Weldon Johnson with John Nail, Fred Moore and the Reverend Frederick Cullen, the unkept Wilson meeting, the petition handed to Joseph Tumulty and the walk to Capitol Hill.

sources.title: Madam Walker's 1917 convention: entrepreneurship, protest, politics
sources.note: Supports the 31 August 1917 agents' convention at Union Baptist Church in Philadelphia, more than two hundred women, Marian Anderson's performance, the telegram to Wilson about Memphis and East St. Louis, the figure of at least thirty-nine African Americans killed in East St. Louis, and the convention prizes.

sources.title: The centennial of Madam C. J. Walker's death, May 25, 1919
sources.note: Supports the date and place of death, age fifty-one, kidney failure, nearly twenty thousand agents, the 30 May funeral at Villa Lewaro with the casket in the music room, J. Rosamond Johnson singing 'Since You Went Away', the 3 June Woodlawn burial, and the pallbearers Fred Moore, J. Rosamond Johnson and Vertner Tandy.

sources.title: Preserving an Iconic Landmark & Business History: Madam C.J. Walker's Villa Lewaro
sources.note: Supports the 1916 commission, 1918 completion, Irvington-on-the-Hudson site, five acres, thirty-four rooms, 20,000 square feet, carriage house, $250,000 cost, Vertner Woodson Tandy as architect, the Caruso naming, the guests including Du Bois, Hughes, Hurston and James Weldon Johnson, and the quotation about providing employment for women of her race.

sources.title: Inventions and Innovations: Entrepreneur Madam C.J. Walker
sources.publisher: Library of Congress, Teaching with the Library
sources.note: Supports Walker's use of Black newspapers to advertise her products and the contemporary ad copy that drew on her working-class origins. Positioned as one of the early female self-made millionaires, not the sole claimant to the title.

sources.title: How Madam C. J. Walker grew a haircare business and made millions
sources.note: Supports the scalp conditions of the period, the sulfur-and-petroleum-jelly type ointments, mixing the early formulas in a washtub, the self-reported dream account, the 1917 millionaire denial and the caution that the famous 'first' and invention claims are not established.

sources.title: Villa Lewaro: the iconic estate
sources.note: Supports the wording of Walker's 1917 denial — 'I am not a millionaire, but I hope to be some day, not because of the money, but because I could do so much to help my race' — the great hall and barrel-vaulted dining room, and the house's Italianate design elements.

sources.title: Who Was the 1st Black Millionairess?
sources.note: Supports the New York Times-attributed washboard reflection — 'What are you going to do when you grow old and your back gets stiff? Who is going to take care of your little girl?' — Frederick Douglass's grandson playing violin at the Villa Lewaro opening, the New York Times obituary headline and the estimates distinguishing personal wealth from company value. The original New York Times interview was not directly accessible in this research pass.
